unmatchedPredictions.title: SQL query built by concatenating the name prefix
unmatchedPredictions.summary: The name prefix passed to findUsersByNamePrefix is concatenated directly into the SQL text on line 14 of src/user-search.ts instead of being passed as a bound parameter. An attacker who controls namePrefix can inject SQL, which can read, change, or delete data in the users table beyond what the search is meant to return.
unmatchedPredictions.remediation: Replace the concatenated string on line 14 with a parameterized query that uses a placeholder for the LIKE pattern, such as WHERE name LIKE ? with the value namePrefix plus "%" supplied as a bound parameter to database.query, and run it through selectUsers.all() with that parameter.
evidence: "SELECT id, name, role FROM users WHERE name LIKE '" + namePrefix + "%'",
unmatchedPredictions.sourceToSink: The namePrefix parameter of the exported findUsersByNamePrefix function is concatenated into the SQL text that database.query prepares and selectUsers.all() executes.

predictedFinding.title: SQL injection through the name query parameter in user search
predictedFinding.summary: The user search in src/server.ts (line 32) builds its SQL by inserting the request's name query parameter directly into the query string. An attacker can supply crafted input that changes the structure of the SQL statement, which is a SQL injection flaw (CWE-89). This can expose or modify data in the users table, including roles, and is rated high severity.
predictedFinding.remediation: Replace the string interpolation on line 32 with a parameterized query, passing the search term as a bound parameter (for example, a placeholder with the value '%' + namePattern + '%' supplied in the parameter array to database.query). Do not concatenate or template user input into SQL text.
evidence: `SELECT id, name, role FROM users WHERE name LIKE '%${namePattern}%'`,
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The name query parameter of the incoming request is interpolated into the SQL string that database.query executes.

predictedFinding.title: DOM XSS from the name query parameter written to innerHTML
predictedFinding.summary: The name query parameter from the page URL is read from window.location and placed directly into an HTML template string that is assigned to innerHTML at public/app.ts line 10. Because the value is not escaped, an attacker can craft a link containing HTML or script markup in the name parameter, which the browser will run in the context of the victim's page. This is a DOM-based cross-site scripting flaw (CWE-79) and can lead to session theft, actions on behalf of the user, or content spoofing.
predictedFinding.remediation: In public/app.ts, stop assigning untrusted text to innerHTML. Build the heading with document.createElement('h1') and set its textContent to the visitor name, then append it to the greeting element. If HTML output is truly required, escape the name value first, but prefer textContent.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The name query parameter of the page URL is read from window.location and interpolated into an HTML string assigned to innerHTML.

predictedFinding.title: OS command injection via host query parameter in ping route
predictedFinding.summary: The ping route takes the host query parameter from the request and drops it straight into a shell command string passed to execSync. An attacker can supply shell metacharacters in host to run arbitrary commands on the server with the application's privileges, which is a critical OS command injection (CWE-78) risk.
predictedFinding.remediation: Stop building the shell string in src/server.ts around lines 104-105. Validate host against a strict allowlist such as a hostname or IP address pattern, and call execFileSync('ping', ['-c', '1', host]) so no shell interprets the input.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The host query parameter of the incoming request is interpolated into the shell command string that execSync runs.

predictedFinding.title: Path traversal in upload download route via name parameter
predictedFinding.summary: The download route takes the name query parameter and joins it onto the uploads directory without checking it. Because Bun.file streams whatever path results, a name containing ../ sequences can escape the uploads directory and read arbitrary files on the server, such as configuration or credentials. This is a path traversal flaw (CWE-22) rated high severity.
predictedFinding.remediation: Resolve the joined path and confirm it still sits inside config.uploadsDirectory before serving it, rejecting the request otherwise. Also reject names containing path separators or .. segments, and return an error instead of streaming the file when the check fails.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The name query parameter of the request is joined onto the uploads directory without validation and Bun.file streams the resulting file, so ../ sequences read arbitrary files.

predictedFinding.title: Bearer token decoded without signature verification
predictedFinding.summary: The bearer token from the Authorization header is decoded with jsonwebtoken.decode, which reads the claims without checking the signature. The userId and role values are then trusted as the session identity, so anyone who can craft a token can impersonate any user or claim any role, including admin. This is a critical authentication bypass (CWE-347).
predictedFinding.remediation: Replace jsonwebtoken.decode with jsonwebtoken.verify, passing the server's signing secret or public key and an explicit algorithms allowlist, so the signature and expiry are checked before userId and role are read. Reject the request when verification fails instead of falling back to the decoded payload.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The bearer token from the Authorization header is read with jsonwebtoken.decode, which does not check the signature, and its userId and role claims are returned as trusted session claims.

predictedFinding.title: SSRF via user-controlled url parameter in /preview
predictedFinding.summary: The /preview handler at src/server.ts (lines 103-106) takes the url query parameter from the incoming request and passes it directly to fetch without any validation. The first 200 characters of whatever the upstream server returns are then sent back to the caller. This is a server-side request forgery (CWE-918): an attacker can make the server send requests to internal hosts, private network addresses, or cloud metadata endpoints and read part of the response, which exposes internal services and data.
predictedFinding.remediation: Parse the url parameter and reject any target that is not on an explicit allowlist of permitted hosts and schemes (for example only https to approved domains). Resolve the hostname and block private, loopback, link-local, and metadata address ranges before calling fetch, and disable or validate redirects so a permitted host cannot redirect to an internal address.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The url query parameter of the incoming request is passed to fetch, and the first 200 characters of the response body are returned to the caller.

predictedFinding.title: Prototype pollution through recursive merge of request JSON
predictedFinding.summary: The recursive merge in src/server.ts (lines 26-27) walks keys from a JSON body posted to /users/:id/preferences without filtering them. A key named "__proto__" lets an attacker reach Object.prototype and write properties onto it, which can change behavior for every object in the running process. This is a prototype pollution flaw (CWE-1321) with medium severity.
predictedFinding.remediation: Update mergeDeep in src/server.ts so it skips the keys "__proto__", "constructor" and "prototype" before reading or writing target[key], and add a test that posts a body containing "__proto__" to /users/:id/preferences and confirms Object.prototype is unchanged.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: A JSON body posted to /users/:id/preferences can contain an own "__proto__" key, which mergeDeep follows via target[key] to Object.prototype and then writes the submitted properties onto it.

predictedFinding.title: eval of expression from request body in /calculate
predictedFinding.summary: The POST /calculate handler in src/server.ts takes the expression field from the client's JSON body and passes it straight to eval, so anyone who can reach the endpoint can run arbitrary JavaScript on the server. This is a critical code injection flaw (CWE-95) that could expose data, change files, or take over the server process.
predictedFinding.remediation: Remove the eval call on line 105 of src/server.ts and replace it with a safe expression parser or a fixed set of allowed arithmetic operations that accepts only numbers and operators. Validate the expression field as a string of allowed characters before using it, and add a test that confirms code such as process or require strings is rejected.
evidence: const calculationBody = (await request.json()) as { expression: string }
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The expression field of the JSON body sent by the client to POST /calculate is passed to eval, which runs it as code on the server.

predictedFinding.title: ms@1.0.0 is affected by GHSA-w9mr-4mfr-499f
predictedFinding.summary: The production dependency ms at version 1.0.0, imported directly by this project, is affected by GHSA-w9mr-4mfr-499f (CVE-2017-20162). A public exploit is reported to exist.
predictedFinding.remediation: Upgrade the ms dependency from 1.0.0 to version 2.0.0 in bun.lock and your package manifest, then rerun your tests to confirm nothing depends on the old behavior.

predictedFinding.title: jws@3.2.2 is affected by GHSA-869p-cjfg-cm3x
predictedFinding.summary: The jws package installed at 3.2.2 (pulled in transitively through jsonwebtoken@9.0.2, a production dependency) is affected by GHSA-869p-cjfg-cm3x / CVE-2025-65945, an improper HMAC signature verification issue. The advisory says exposure requires the application to use jws.createVerify() for HMAC algorithms and to pass user-provided header or payload data into the HMAC secret lookup. Applications that use jws.verify() (which includes jsonwebtoken users), use only asymmetric algorithms, or do not feed user-controlled data into secret lookups are not affected. Whether this project meets those conditions needs to be checked.
predictedFinding.remediation: Upgrade jws to version 3.2.3 (or 4.0.1 if moving to the 4.x line) so the transitive dependency under jsonwebtoken@9.0.2 is no longer 3.2.2, then regenerate bun.lock. Also confirm that the code does not call jws.createVerify() with HMAC secrets derived from user-supplied token data.

predictedFinding.title: path-to-regexp@0.1.11 is affected by GHSA-rhx6-c78j-4q9w
predictedFinding.summary: The bun.lock file pins path-to-regexp at version 0.1.11, which is affected by GHSA-rhx6-c78j-4q9w (CVE-2024-52798), a regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) issue caused by catastrophic backtracking in generated regular expressions. The dependency is a production scope dependency, but the advisory report marks it as directly present and currently unused, so exploitation risk depends on whether it is reached at runtime. An attacker able to supply crafted input could still cause excessive CPU use if the vulnerable pattern path is exercised.
predictedFinding.remediation: Upgrade path-to-regexp to version 0.1.12 in the project and regenerate bun.lock so the lockfile records the fixed version. As an interim mitigation, avoid defining two parameters within a single path segment when the separator is not a dot (for example, avoid /:a-:b).

predictedFinding.title: Input length cap raised 100x in front of a backtracking regex
predictedFinding.summary: The input length cap in front of the parse function was raised from 100 to 10000 characters. The value passed in is then matched against a regular expression whose overlapping digit quantifiers can backtrack quadratically on a long run of digits followed by an invalid suffix. A 100x larger input makes that slowdown about 10000x worse, so a single crafted request can tie up the process for a long time (CWE-1333, regular expression denial of service).
predictedFinding.remediation: Restore the input length cap to its previous lower limit, or rewrite the regex so the digit quantifiers do not overlap (for example, match a single digit run such as \d*\.?\d+ without the optional repeated group) and add a test with a long digit string plus an invalid suffix to confirm parse returns quickly.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The str argument passed to parse is now allowed up to 10000 characters before reaching the regex `^((?:\d+)?\.?\d+) *(...)?$`, whose overlapping `\d+` quantifiers backtrack quadratically on a long digit string with an invalid suffix.

predictedFinding.title: Regex with nested overlapping quantifiers on host causes ReDoS
predictedFinding.summary: On line 122 of src/utils/referrer.js, the URL host from an attacker-controlled referrer is tested with /^(.+\.)*localhost$/. The group (.+\.)* has overlapping quantifiers, because the dot-matching part can also match the literal dots. When the host is a long dotted string that does not end in localhost, the regex engine backtracks exponentially. A crafted referrer can then stall the thread that processes it, which is a denial of service (CWE-1333, ReDoS).
predictedFinding.remediation: Replace the regex test on line 122 with a plain string check that cannot backtrack, such as url.host === 'localhost' || url.host.endsWith('.localhost'), and confirm that the existing localhost behavior is preserved. Then add a test with a long dotted host that does not end in localhost to confirm it returns quickly.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The host of an attacker-controlled referrer URL is tested against the regex /^(.+\.)*localhost$/, whose (.+\.)* group has overlapping quantifiers that backtrack exponentially on a long dotted host that does not end in localhost.

predictedFinding.title: Locale name path check removed before dynamic require
predictedFinding.summary: A caller-supplied locale name passed to loadLocale is no longer checked for path separators ('/' or '\') before it is used in a dynamic require of a locale file path. This opens a path traversal risk (CWE-22), where a crafted locale name could point the require at files outside the intended locale directory.
predictedFinding.remediation: Restore the check that rejects locale names containing '/' or '\' before the dynamic require in src/lib/locale/locales.js near line 73, and also validate the locale name against an allowlist of known locale identifiers before calling require.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: A caller-supplied locale name passed to loadLocale is no longer checked for '/' or '\' and then reaches the existing dynamic require of a locale file path.

predictedFinding.title: GitHub token added in .github/workflows/deploy.yml
predictedFinding.summary: A GitHub token is hardcoded in the workflow file .github/workflows/deploy.yml at line 13. Anyone who can read the repository, or its git history, can copy the token and use it with whatever permissions it grants, which could allow access to code or deployments. Because the value is now in version control, treat it as compromised even if the line is later removed.
predictedFinding.remediation: Revoke the exposed token in GitHub immediately and issue a replacement with the least permissions needed. Remove the literal value from line 13 of .github/workflows/deploy.yml and reference the new token as a repository or environment secret, such as ${{ secrets.YOUR_SECRET_NAME }}. Then check the repository's git history and purge the old value if your policy requires it.

predictedFinding.title: Private key block added in deploy/key.pem
predictedFinding.summary: A private key block was added in deploy/key.pem. Anyone with access to this repository or its history can read the key, which could let them impersonate the service or decrypt data protected by it. This is rated critical because the secret is now exposed in version control.
predictedFinding.remediation: Remove the private key from deploy/key.pem in this change, then rotate the key so the exposed one is no longer trusted. Load the key at deploy time from a secrets manager or environment variable instead of committing it to the repository.

predictedFinding.title: Input length cap raised 100x in front of a backtracking regex
predictedFinding.summary: The input length cap in front of the parse function was raised from 100 to 10000 characters. The value passed in is then matched against a regular expression whose overlapping digit quantifiers can backtrack quadratically on a long run of digits followed by an invalid suffix. A 100x larger input makes that slowdown about 10000x worse, so a single crafted request can tie up the process for a long time (CWE-1333, regular expression denial of service).
predictedFinding.remediation: Restore the input length cap to its previous lower limit, or rewrite the regex so the digit quantifiers do not overlap (for example, match a single digit run such as \d*\.?\d+ without the optional repeated group) and add a test with a long digit string plus an invalid suffix to confirm parse returns quickly.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The str argument passed to parse is now allowed up to 10000 characters before reaching the regex `^((?:\d+)?\.?\d+) *(...)?$`, whose overlapping `\d+` quantifiers backtrack quadratically on a long digit string with an invalid suffix.

predictedFinding.title: Regex with nested overlapping quantifiers on host causes ReDoS
predictedFinding.summary: On line 122 of src/utils/referrer.js, the URL host from an attacker-controlled referrer is tested with /^(.+\.)*localhost$/. The group (.+\.)* has overlapping quantifiers, because the dot-matching part can also match the literal dots. When the host is a long dotted string that does not end in localhost, the regex engine backtracks exponentially. A crafted referrer can then stall the thread that processes it, which is a denial of service (CWE-1333, ReDoS).
predictedFinding.remediation: Replace the regex test on line 122 with a plain string check that cannot backtrack, such as url.host === 'localhost' || url.host.endsWith('.localhost'), and confirm that the existing localhost behavior is preserved. Then add a test with a long dotted host that does not end in localhost to confirm it returns quickly.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The host of an attacker-controlled referrer URL is tested against the regex /^(.+\.)*localhost$/, whose (.+\.)* group has overlapping quantifiers that backtrack exponentially on a long dotted host that does not end in localhost.

predictedFinding.title: Locale name path check removed before dynamic require
predictedFinding.summary: A caller-supplied locale name passed to loadLocale is no longer checked for path separators ('/' or '\') before it is used in a dynamic require of a locale file path. This opens a path traversal risk (CWE-22), where a crafted locale name could point the require at files outside the intended locale directory.
predictedFinding.remediation: Restore the check that rejects locale names containing '/' or '\' before the dynamic require in src/lib/locale/locales.js near line 73, and also validate the locale name against an allowlist of known locale identifiers before calling require.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: A caller-supplied locale name passed to loadLocale is no longer checked for '/' or '\' and then reaches the existing dynamic require of a locale file path.
